whyThisMatters: In a real incident, most people freeze or try to fix it alone. The habit that helps is knowing your next step before you need it, whether you work in an office, at home or on the move.
rememberThis: The one line to take away: STOP, VERIFY, REPORT. Use this order every time, no matter how the situation looks.

discussionPrompts: Ask the group what they would do in the first few seconds of each scenario, before showing the good answer.
For the phone-call case, ask if anyone knows a trusted number by heart to call back on, or would have to look it up under pressure.
Ask why "wait and see if anything goes wrong" feels tempting, even though it is the wrong choice in every case here.
Ask how it felt to decide under time pressure. Was it harder to pause when the clock was running?
For the video-call case, ask if anyone would feel okay ending a call with a senior leader to go and check.
Ask the group to name their own trusted way to check an urgent request, such as a known phone number or a manager.
facilitatorNotes.commonWrongAnswer: The most common mistake is trying to fix it yourself before reporting, such as changing a password or deleting a message. It feels helpful but can destroy evidence IT needs. People also often fail the video-call case by approving the payment because the face and voice matched.

cases.title: You Clicked a Link in an Email
cases.scenario: You are catching up on email. You click a link in a message called "Re: Your document is ready to view". The page that opens looks odd and a login box appears. Phishing means a fake message designed to trick you into clicking or giving away details.

decisions.prompt: The page asks you to log in again. What do you do first?

options.text: Type your work password to see if it is real
options.feedback: Never type a password on a page you doubt. Even a quick test can hand your login to attackers.

options.text: Close the tab, type nothing, and tell the IT helpdesk right away
options.feedback: Right choice. Typing nothing stops the attack, and a fast report lets IT check your account before any damage is done.

options.text: Take a screenshot and ask a colleague what they think before doing anything else
options.feedback: Asking colleagues first only wastes time. The key step is telling IT fast.

cases.debrief: Clicking is easy to do and common. STOP before you type anything. VERIFY by going to the real site yourself if you are unsure. REPORT to the IT helpdesk straight away. Every minute counts.

cases.title: The Invoice With New Bank Details
cases.scenario: An email arrives from a supplier you know: "Please note our bank details have changed. Pay this week's invoice to the new account below." The invoice looks real and the logo is correct. This trick is called business email compromise, where attackers pose as a supplier to redirect payments.

options.text: Pay it using the new details, since the invoice looks normal
options.feedback: A convincing invoice proves nothing. Paying the wrong account usually means the money is gone.

options.text: Do not pay yet. Call the supplier on a number you already have on file, and report the email to IT
options.feedback: Right call. Checking by a trusted second channel defeats the scam, and reporting helps protect your colleagues.

options.text: Reply to the email asking if the new details are correct
options.feedback: Replying goes to the sender, who may be the attacker. They will simply say yes.

cases.debrief: STOP before you act. VERIFY through a channel you already trust, never the one the sender gave you. REPORT it to the IT helpdesk.

cases.title: You Found a USB Stick
cases.scenario: You find a small USB stick (a thumb drive) on the floor near the meeting rooms. It has no label and no owner in sight. You are curious what is on it.

options.text: Plug it into your computer to see who owns it
options.feedback: Never plug in a found device. It can install harmful software the moment it connects.

options.text: Do not plug it in. Hand it to the IT helpdesk or security and report where you found it
options.feedback: Right. IT can inspect it safely, and the location may show someone left it there on purpose.

options.text: Plug it into an old shared computer that is not important
options.feedback: Any connected computer can be harmed and then spread the problem across the network.

cases.debrief: Attackers leave devices as bait. STOP, do not plug it in. VERIFY nothing yourself, because only IT can check it safely. REPORT it to IT or security.

cases.title: The Urgent Call From a Senior Leader
cases.scenario: You join a video call. A senior leader appears and asks you to send an urgent payment today and to keep it confidential. The face and voice seem right. Deepfakes are fake audio or video made with AI that can copy a real person.

decisions.prompt: The leader pushes you to act before the end of the day. What do you do?

options.text: Approve the payment, because it is clearly them
options.feedback: Voice and video can now be faked. Looking right is not proof.

options.text: Ask them to send the details by email and do it from there
options.feedback: Email can also be faked, and this does not independently check the request.

options.text: Pause, then confirm by calling them on a number you already trust, and follow the normal payment process
options.feedback: Right. A second trusted channel, plus normal approvals, defeats the pressure. A real leader will not mind.

options.text: Ask a teammate whether it looks genuine, then pay
options.feedback: Your teammate sees the same fake. Check with the person directly through a trusted route.

cases.debrief: Urgency and secrecy are warning signs. STOP, even if it is a senior person. VERIFY on a known number. REPORT the attempt to IT or security so others are warned.

cases.title: Your Work Laptop Is Missing
cases.scenario: After a business trip you realise your work laptop is not in your bag. You may have left it in a taxi. It holds customer files and you are logged in to your work accounts.

options.text: Wait a day or two in case it turns up
options.feedback: Every hour matters. A lost laptop can be accessed quickly if it is not locked or wiped.

options.text: Report it to the IT helpdesk straight away so they can lock or wipe it and reset your access
options.feedback: Right. A quick report lets IT remotely lock the device and protect company and customer data.

cases.debrief: Lost devices are common and reportable. STOP, do not just hope. VERIFY what was on it if you can, such as files and accounts. REPORT to IT at once, and do not worry about blame.

cases.title: Pasting Data Into an AI Tool
cases.scenario: You want a quick summary of a customer list and a contract. A free public AI chatbot would do it in seconds, but the files contain names, emails and prices. Data you paste into some AI tools can be stored or used to train them.

options.text: Paste everything into the public AI tool to save time
options.feedback: Pasting private data into a public tool means you lose control of it. It may be stored outside the company.

options.text: Remove the names only, then paste the rest
options.feedback: Details like prices and context can still identify the customer or the deal.

options.text: Use only the AI tool your company has approved, or ask IT first, and share only what policy allows
options.feedback: Right. Approved tools have agreed data protections. Asking first keeps customer information safe.

options.text: Use your personal phone so it is not on the work computer
options.feedback: The data still leaves the company. A different device does not make it safe.

cases.debrief: Treat AI tools like a stranger who may remember. STOP before pasting. VERIFY the tool is approved and the data is allowed. REPORT to IT if you already pasted something you should not have.

cases.title: A Colleague Asks to Borrow Your Login
cases.scenario: A new colleague has not received system access yet. They ask to use your username and password for the day so they can get started. They seem friendly and say everyone does it.

options.text: Share your password this once to help them
options.feedback: Shared passwords mean no one can tell who did what. If something goes wrong, you are the one on record.

options.text: Politely refuse and ask your manager or the IT helpdesk to speed up their access
options.feedback: Right. Everyone should have their own login. IT can often fast-track a new starter quickly.

cases.debrief: Passwords are personal. STOP before sharing. VERIFY by asking the manager or IT for proper access. REPORT if anyone pressures you into sharing. If you already shared it, change it and tell IT.

cases.title: The Person Behind You at the Door
cases.scenario: You badge in at a secure office door. A person you do not recognise follows closely, carrying coffee. They say, "Sorry, forgot my pass, can you hold the door?" This is called tailgating, following someone through a secure door without a badge.

options.text: Hold the door, since they look friendly and carry coffee
options.feedback: Looking normal is exactly how tailgaters get in. Kindness here can open the building to anyone.

options.text: Politely say you cannot let them in, and direct them to reception or call security
options.feedback: Right. Reception can check who they are. Polite and firm is a good habit, and nobody genuine will mind.

options.text: Let them in and ask for their name after
options.feedback: A name is easy to make up and they are already inside.

options.text: Say nothing and let them in, assuming someone else will check
options.feedback: Everyone assuming someone else will check is how gaps appear.

cases.debrief: Physical security matters as much as digital. STOP before holding the door. VERIFY through reception or security. REPORT a stranger inside the building.

cases.title: A Call From "IT Support"
cases.scenario: Your phone rings. The caller says they are from IT support and your account is under attack. To fix it, they need the six-digit code that was just sent to your phone. Vishing is voice phishing, a scam done by phone.

options.text: Read out the code, since they are trying to help
options.feedback: That code is the key to your account. Real IT staff never need to ask you for it.

options.text: Say no, hang up, and call the IT helpdesk on the official number to check and report it
options.feedback: Right. Hanging up and calling a number you already trust beats any caller pressure.

cases.debrief: Never share a code or password by phone. STOP when someone creates panic. VERIFY by calling back on an official number you find yourself. REPORT it to IT.

cases.title: Working From a Cafe
cases.scenario: You are working from a cafe and need to send a confidential file. The cafe Wi-Fi is open with no password, and you see two similar names: "CafeFreeWiFi" and "Cafe_Guest". Open Wi-Fi can be copied by attackers to watch what you send.

options.text: Connect to the strongest signal and send the file
options.feedback: You cannot tell which network is real. A fake one can capture your traffic.

options.text: Use your phone hotspot or the company VPN, and keep confidential work for a safer place
options.feedback: Right. A VPN or your own hotspot keeps your traffic private. Waiting is safer than guessing.

options.text: Send the file, since the website has a padlock
options.feedback: The padlock does not protect you from a fake network or a copied login page.

cases.debrief: Remote work still needs the same habits. STOP before joining unknown Wi-Fi. VERIFY by using a VPN or hotspot. REPORT anything odd, such as unexpected login prompts, to IT.
